Response to comment 7:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and crucial comment. The practical
viability of any new material for atmospheric water harvesting is indeed contingent
upon its economic feasibility, production scalability, and long-term sustainability. We
acknowledge that our original manuscript did not adequately address these aspects. To
address this issue, we have added a new paragraph in the “Demonstration of the outdoor
water-harvesting tests” section regarding future prospects, specifically to discuss these
problems.
Below, we have conducted a detailed analysis from the three perspectives
mentioned by the reviewer to ensure that the proposed system is placed within the
broader landscape of atmospheric water harvesting.
1. Cost-Effectiveness of Raw Materials
A key advantage of our HPGP organogel lies in the intrinsic low cost and wide
availability of its primary components.
Pectin, the outer shell in this system, is a natural polysaccharide extracted
commercially from citrus peels and apple pomace, which are abundant byproducts of
the food processing industry. Its current market price is relatively low (typically in the
range of $15-30 per kilogram for industrial grades), making it a highly cost-effective
substrate for large-scale applications. Its food-grade status also ensures its inherent
safety and biocompatibility (Fig. R3). [1]
Fig. R3 The Wide-Ranging Sources and Applications of Pectin. [2]
Graphene Oxide, the intermediate layer in this system, while research-grade GO
can be expensive, the cost for industrial-scale production has plummeted in recent years.
GO is synthesized from natural graphite, a globally abundant and inexpensive carbon
source. The modified Hummers method, which we employed, is the most common and
scalable process for graphite oxidation. With process optimization and economies of
scale, the production cost of GO is projected to fall significantly, making it a viable
component for bulk materials like ours. [3] Glycerol, the liquid phase entity in the
system, as a major byproduct of the biodiesel industry, crude glycerol is inexpensive
and globally oversupplied. While purification adds cost, industrial-grade glycerol
remains a very affordable liquid sorbent. [4]
The reliance on earth-abundant, industry-byproduct, or natural raw materials
positions the HPGP system as a fundamentally low-cost technology, which is a critical
prerequisite for its deployment, especially in resource-limited regions.
2. Production Scalability
First, concerning the reproducibility of the crucial wrinkle structure, we can
confirm its high consistency over extended periods. The formation of these wrinkles is
governed by a well-understood physical mechanism: strain mismatch arising from the
iterative drying and differential shrinkage of the GO layers. The primary determinants
of the wrinkle wavelength and amplitude are the material’s modulus and the final dry
film thickness, which are directly controlled by the GO solution concentration and the
number of deposition-drying cycles. Systematic experiments show that a four-layer
structure consistently forms the optimal wrinkle pattern. This conclusion is supported
by the macroscopic images of samples prepared at different times from December 2022
to the present, all of which exhibit a consistent wrinkle pattern (Supplementary Fig. 58).
Similarly, regarding layer uniformity, we have conducted rigorous quality control
throughout our research. Thickness measurements of the GO base films, also performed
on samples from different batches over the same extended timeframe, confirm excellent
uniformity with minimal deviation (Supplementary Fig. 59). This consistency
underscores the robustness of our layer-by-layer assembly protocol, where controlled
solution spreading and drying steps ensure a uniform deposition process.
Supplementary Fig. 58 From December 2022 to December 2025, the GO film has a stable wrinkle
structure.
Supplementary Fig. 59 The GO film from December 2022 to December 2025 has a uniform
thickness.
Finally, we have carefully considered the feasibility of mass production and
envision a clear pathway to translate our laboratory-scale “spread-dry-repeat” method
into an industrially relevant, continuous process (Supplementary Fig. 57). The four-
layer GO base film can be formed using established techniques such as spray/blade
coating or slot-die coating, coupled with a multi-zone hot-air drying system to perform
the iterative deposition cycles. Following the formation of the base film, the surface
pectin layers would be applied to both sides using a similar coating process.
Subsequently, the functionalization steps can be adapted to an in-line configuration: the
cross-linking would occur in a short-residence-time anhydrous zinc acetate bath, and
the final glycerol solvent exchange could be managed in a counter-current washing
cascade to enhance throughput and reduce solvent consumption.
It is important to highlight that all the aforementioned steps—coating, multi-zone
drying, and immersion baths—are standard unit operations within the membrane and
coating industries. Key process parameters such as coating speed, drying temperature
and humidity, and residence time can be precisely controlled to replicate the thermal
history and layering effect achieved in our lab. Given that our entire process utilizes
aqueous solutions, operates at ambient or mild temperatures, and requires no high-
vacuum or cleanroom facilities, we are confident that scaling this fabrication from
centimeter-sized lab samples to meter-scale roll-to-roll production is engineeringly
feasible. While we refrain from adding new scale-up data in the current manuscript to
maintain focus, we have supplemented the methods section with more explicit process
parameters and quality control metrics. This will ensure that our peers can readily
replicate the material’s unique morphology and high performance under equivalent
conditions.
Supplementary Fig. 57 Simulated large-scale factory preparation process for HPGP.
3. Material Recyclability and Sustainability
The unique heterogeneous design of our HPGP not only enhances performance but
also offers significant advantages in terms of sustainability and end-of-life management.
Mechanical Disassembly: As demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 51, the HPGP
structure is not permanently bonded and can be mechanically delaminated. This
physical separation is a crucial feature for recycling. After a long service life, the
material can be disassembled into its constituent layers.
Supplementary Fig. 51 HPGP can be disassembled in layers by external force.
Component-Specific End-of-Life Pathways:
Pectin layer: Being a natural biomass material, the pectin layers are
fully biodegradable, as shown in our soil degradation test (Supplementary Fig. 52). This
allows for a safe and environmentally benign disposal route, returning the organic
matter to the ecosystem.
Supplementary Fig. 52 The pectin layer can be broken down naturally by placing it in the soil.
GO layer: The GO interlayer is chemically robust and stable. After separation, it
can be washed, potentially reactivated (if fouled), and directly reused to fabricate new
HPGP films. This recyclability of the most energy-intensive component significantly
improves the material’s life-cycle assessment and reduces overall waste
(Supplementary Fig. 53).
Supplementary Fig. 53 Morphology before and after sample moisture sorption cycle.
This disassembly-and-reuse potential creates a pathway for a circular economy
model for the SAWH system. Instead of disposing of the entire device, the core
functional material (GO) can be recovered and repurposed, minimizing environmental
impact and long-term material costs.
Our design thoughtfully incorporates end-of-life considerations. The combination
of a biodegradable shell and a recyclable functional core makes the HPGP material
highly sustainable and aligns with the principles of a circular economy.

Comment 1:
In the last paragraph of the Introduction, please clarify how the GO interlayer amplifies
glycerol-generated osmotic pumping as the glycerol appears suddenly from the
structure (pectin-GO-pectin). We can tell that glycerin is used from Figure S1, but we
cannot get clear information about glycerin in the Introduction, such as where is it, why
it is needed, etc. Also, please highlight why the proposed structure can address the
research gap mentioned above.
Response to comment 1:
Thank you for this critical question, which highlights a logical gap in our previous
explanation. We acknowledge that simply stating the GO interlayer “amplifies” the
osmotic effect is insufficient. The GO interlayer does not increase the intrinsic osmotic
potential of glycerol, but rather sustains the effectiveness of this potential over time
by overcoming the kinetic limitations inherent in homogeneous structure. We have
thoroughly re-evaluated this point and revised the manuscript to provide a more precise,
mechanism-driven explanation.
The central challenge in sorption-based atmospheric water harvesting that our
work addresses is the inherent trade-off between sorption capacity and water
transport kinetics. Conventional homogeneous structure typically rely on
homogeneous hydrophilic networks. While these materials are effective at capturing
water molecules via strong hydrogen bonding, this same interaction severely restricts
the mobility of the captured water, leading to low diffusion coefficients within the
material’s bulk. Initially, the glycerol infused throughout the material creates a powerful
osmotic gradient that drives water vapor uptake. However, as water molecules are
captured by the hydrophilic polymer matrix (pectin), they become kinetically trapped
within a dense hydrogen-bond network. This rapidly saturates the surface, creating a
diffusion barrier that drastically reduces the osmotic pressure gradient at the air-
material interface and throttles further water uptake (Fig. 2a, b).
In our heterogeneous design, glycerol is infused throughout the composite, where
it functions as a potent hygroscopic substance. Its primary role is to establish a large
osmotic pressure gradient at the air-material interface, creating the thermodynamic
driving force for the efficient capture of atmospheric water vapor and its condensation
into a liquid state. This glycerol-driven osmotic pump is then amplified by the central
graphene oxide (GO) interlayer, which provides a kinetic solution to sustain the
pump’s high efficiency. When captured water molecules reach the interface with the
GO interlayer, they transition from a strongly bound state within the hydrophilic pectin
matrix to a more mobile, free state along the low-friction surfaces of the GO nanosheets.
This rapid translocation of liquid water from the surface to the material's interior
continuously vacates active sorption sites in the outer pectin layer. By preventing the
formation of a saturation barrier, the GO network ensures that the potent osmotic
gradient established by glycerol remains consistently exposed to the humid air, thereby
sustaining a high water vapor flux into the material. This dynamic interplay—where
glycerol provides the thermodynamic driving force for capture and the GO interlayer
provides the kinetic pathway for sustained transport—is what constitutes the
amplification of the overall sorption kinetics.
Fig. 2 a, In conventional homogeneous structure, the hydrogen-bonded disordered
network imposes dual spatial confinement on water molecules via steric hindrance and
intermolecular attraction. b, Heterogeneous structure enables high-speed water diffusion through
GO nanosheets following water molecule traversal across the hydrogen-bonded network.
This functionally-decoupled design directly addresses the research gap by
breaking the sorption-transport compromise. We validate this mechanism through a
synergistic combination of computational modeling and experimental evidence. Our
Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations provide the theoretical basis, revealing that
water molecules exhibit a significantly higher diffusion coefficient within our
heterogeneous structure (204.03) compared to a homogeneous analog (181.16),
confirming the role of GO as a high-speed conduit. To experimentally verify this, we
conducted low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF-NMR) T relaxation experiments,
2
a technique that distinguishes between motion-restricted “bound water” and highly
mobile “free water”. The LF-NMR results provide direct experimental proof of two
distinct water populations (Supplementary Fig. 13). At low humidity, we observed only
a signal corresponding to bound water, confirming that initial uptake is dominated by
strong immobilization within the hydrophilic pectin-glycerol layers
(Supplementary Fig. 13a, b). Crucially, at high humidity, a new, distinct peak emerged,
representing a population of free, mobile water (Supplementary Fig. 13d). This
mobile water population is the direct experimental signature of the rapid transport
occurring within the GO interlayer, as predicted by our MD simulations. The LF-NMR
data confirms the existence of two distinct water states, while the MD simulations
explain the underlying mechanism of low-friction transport in the GO nanochannels.
This synergy between experiments and theory provides validation for our design,
demonstrating that the spatial decoupling of water capture (bound water in pectin) and
transport (free water in GO) effectively balances the trade-off between sorption
capacity and water transport kinetics.

Response to comment 3:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful question, which touches upon the
fundamental mechanics of GO interlayers formation. The observed decrease in surface
wrinkles as the number of GO interlayers increases (as shown in Figure S35, now on
Supplementary Fig. 61) is indeed a direct consequence of the relationship between the
film’s bending stiffness and its thickness.
The initial wrinkle is established on the first four layers (Supplementary Fig. 60),
driven by drying-induced stresses that cause the thin film to buckle. However, as each
subsequent GO layer is added, the total thickness of the multilayer film increases.
In classical mechanics, the bending stiffness (or flexural rigidity) of a plate or a film is
proportional to the cube of its thickness:

12
where EI represents the flexural rigidity, b represents the cross-sectional width, and h
represents the cross-sectional thickness. Therefore, with each new layer, the overall
bending stiffness of the GO interlayers increases dramatically. This rapidly increasing
stiffness has a profound effect, which makes the film progressively more resistant to
deformation. The internal stresses generated during the drying of a new, thin top layer
are no longer sufficient to buckle or significantly deform the much thicker and stiffer
substrate beneath it. Instead of forming new high-amplitude wrinkles, the composite
film is now rigid enough to maintain a flatter configuration. The slight, remaining
contractile forces from the top layer might induce very low-amplitude, high-frequency
micro-wrinkles, but the dominant, larger wrinkles from the initial layers are effectively
locked in and suppressed by the sheer mechanical rigidity of the thickening film. In
essence, while the initial layers are flexible enough to buckle into a wrinkled state, the
subsequent layers are deposited onto a substrate that becomes increasingly rigid,
preventing further large-scale deformation and leading to a progressively smoother
surface.

We thank the reviewer for your meticulous reading of the manuscript and for
highlighting these important points that require correction and clarification. We have

First and foremost, we sincerely apologize for the incorrect figure reference on

Regarding the mechanism of how GO layers help “reduce the interaction
between water molecules and hydrophilic groups (pectin),” we recognize that our
previous description may have been misleading. To be more precise, the role of the GO
layers is not to weaken the inherent hydrophilicity of pectin, but rather to structurally
optimize the transport pathway for water molecules. As mentioned in the manuscript,
in a conventional homogeneous structure, excessive hydrogen bonding immobilizes
water molecules within the pectin chain network, thereby restricting their mobility (Fig.
2a, b). In our designed heterogeneous structure, however, the GO interlayers serve as
relatively hydrophobic fast channels that physically separate the moisture-capturing
pectin layer from the water storage regions. After the outer pectin layer captures and
liquefies water vapor, these liquid water molecules, driven by the osmotic pressure
generated by glycerol, can diffuse rapidly along the GO interlayer interfaces to the
interior. This pathway allows them to effectively bypass the slow percolation process
through the pectin network itself. Therefore, by constructing independent, low-
resistance transport pathways, the GO layers circumvent the kinetic limitations imposed
by excessive hydrogen bonding in a homogeneous network, thereby accelerating the
overall water transport dynamics.
Fig. 2 a, In conventional homogeneous structure, the hydrogen-bonded disordered
network imposes dual spatial confinement on water molecules via steric hindrance and
intermolecular attraction. b, Heterogeneous structure enables high-speed water diffusion through
GO nanosheets following water molecule traversal across the hydrogen-bonded network.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for your meticulous examination of our molecular
dynamics (MD) simulations and for raising this insightful question. It provides us with
a valuable opportunity to elaborate on the scientific rationale behind our simulation
models. The reviewer correctly observed that our MD model for the heterogeneous
structure (Fig. 3b) does not explicitly show pectin molecules, whereas the model for
the homogeneous structure (Fig. 3c) does. This was not an oversight, but a deliberate
simplification strategy designed to effectively test our core scientific hypothesis.
Our central hypothesis is that in a conventional homogeneous structure, the dense
hydrogen-bonding network formed by the high degree of entanglement between pectin
chains and GO nanosheets is the primary barrier to the rapid diffusion of water
molecules. To verify this, we constructed the homogeneous model shown in Fig. 3c. In
this model, we explicitly included pectin molecules (represented as yellow chains)
intermixed with GO and water molecules. The purpose was to recreate this congested
and sterically hindered environment at the atomic scale, allowing us to directly observe
and quantify the restrictive effect of the pectin chains on the diffusion of water
molecules (blue spheres). The simulation results clearly demonstrate that water
molecule mobility is severely limited in this environment, thus validating our
hypothesis.
In contrast, the core principle of our heterogeneous structure (HPGP) design is the
physical, layered separation of the main diffusion pathway (the GO interlayers) from
the highly hydrophilic pectin layer. After passing through the hydrophilic pectin
“capture layer” on the surface, water molecules primarily diffuse rapidly within the
relatively independent and smooth GO interlayer channels. To clearly highlight the
advantage of this “fast channel” in our simulation, we constructed the heterogeneous
model shown in Fig. 3b. The central purpose of this model is to simulate the diffusion
behavior of water molecules after they have entered the GO interlayer space. At this
stage, according to our design, pectin is located on the exterior of the GO framework
and does not participate in the core transport process within the interlayers. Therefore,
to emphasize the intrinsic feature of the GO layers as independent, low-resistance
channels and to create the most direct and stark contrast with the homogeneous model,
we omitted pectin from the model in Fig. 3b. This simplification allows us to clearly
isolate the impact of the structure on the diffusion kinetics and to demonstrate that by
constructing independent GO channels, the diffusion coefficient of water molecules can
be significantly enhanced.
In summary, our differential treatment of pectin in the two models was a
purposeful design choice based on their respective simulation objectives. The
homogeneous model (Fig. 3c) includes pectin to demonstrate its impeding role in water
diffusion within a mixed system, while the heterogeneous model (Fig. 3b) omits pectin
from the channel to highlight the decisive advantage of the independent GO pathway
in promoting water diffusion. The MD simulation results (as indicated by the
differences in diffusion coefficients, with the MSD for the heterogeneous structure
being 204.03 and for the homogeneous structure being 181.18) strongly support our
core argument. We acknowledge that our explanation in the original manuscript was
not sufficiently detailed, and we have now added the necessary clarifications to the
manuscript to ensure that readers can accurately understand the scientific intent behind
our models.

Supplementary Fig. 11 documents the dynamic process within the heterogeneous
system over a 1000 ps simulation. The initial frame (0 ps) depicts an artificially ordered
arrangement of water molecules and graphene oxide (GO) sheets, a standard starting
point for such simulations. As the simulation progresses, the subsequent snapshots
reveal the system relaxing into a more physically realistic, equilibrated state. We
observe the formation of well-defined, continuous water channels between the GO
layers. By the end of the simulation, while individual molecules remain in constant
motion, the overall structure maintains stable, unobstructed pathways. This visual
evidence substantiates the concept that the layered architecture facilitates rapid, low-
resistance water transport, providing a physical rationale for the high diffusion
coefficients we report.
In contrast, Supplementary Fig. 10 illustrates the dynamic evolution of the
homogeneous system. This simulation also begins from an ordered initial state, but the
subsequent process is markedly different. The snapshots show the flexible pectin chains
becoming progressively entangled with each other and forming a dense, hydrogen-
bonded network that incorporates both the water molecules and the GO surface. Instead
of forming clear channels, the system evolves into a congested and tortuous matrix. The
later frames of the simulation show that water molecules are effectively trapped within
this amorphous polymer network, with their mobility severely restricted. This provides
a direct visual confirmation of our hypothesis that the dense, intertwined nature of a
homogeneous structure creates a high-resistance environment that fundamentally
hinders water diffusion. Together, these figures offer a compelling qualitative
comparison, starkly contrasting the ordered, high-mobility environment of the
heterogeneous structure with the disordered, low-mobility environment of its
homogeneous counterpart, thereby reinforcing the conclusions drawn from our
quantitative analysis.

Finally, concerning the non-leakage property of the HPGP, its guarantee
stems from a combination of its crosslinked network structure and strong capillary
forces. First, at the molecular level, the pectin layers are ionically crosslinked by Zn2+
ions, forming a stable hydrogel network that securely entraps the hygroscopic liquid.
Second, at the microstructural level, the nanochannels between the GO layers and the
wrinkled surface topography generate powerful capillary forces that firmly lock the
liquid mixture within the material’s internal structure. This dual-force system is
sufficiently strong to overcome gravity, effectively preventing any liquid leakage even
when the material reaches its maximum water uptake of 6.57 g g-1. To further
demonstrate that no leakage occurs, we conducted a series of supplementary
experiments.
First, to simulate real-world handling and mechanical stress, we conducted a
centrifugation test. The fully glycerol-infused HPGP organogel was weighed and then
subjected to high-speed centrifugation (e.g., at 3000 rpm for 30 minutes). After the test,
the sample was reweighed. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 22, there was only a 0.005g
loss in mass before and after centrifugation, confirming that even under significant
gravitational acceleration, the liquid was not expelled from the matrix, demonstrating
its excellent physical liquid-retention capability.

any signs of liquid staining or wetness, which would indicate glycerol leakage.
Concurrently, the mass of the hydrogel was monitored. We observed no visual signs of

careful re-examination of our data, particularly the desorption curves in Figure 5f, in
conjunction with our new thermal imaging evidence, allows us to provide a more
precise and physically grounded distinction between “surface heating” and “internal
heating” and a clearer operational definition of desorption onset.
The terms “surface heating” and “internal heating” are used to describe the
primary thermal transport dynamics within the two distinct material architectures: the
homogeneous and our proposed heterogeneous structure, respectively. “Surface
heating” characterizes the behavior of the homogeneous control sample, where the
photothermal GO is uniformly blended with the pectin. As confirmed by our new cross-
sectional thermal imaging, under illumination, heat is generated predominantly at the
top surface, which is directly exposed to the light source. This heat must then conduct
slowly downward through the insulating, water-saturated hydrogel matrix. This
inefficient “outside-in” heat transfer results in a significant thermal lag for the bulk
of the material and substantial energy loss to the environment from the hot surface. In
stark contrast, “internal heating” describes the unique mechanism of our
heterogeneous design. Here, the GO interlayer acts as a dedicated, centralized heat
source, strategically embedded within the gel. The largely transparent top pectin layer
allows light to penetrate to this internal core, which then heats up and radiates thermal
energy outwards in both directions. This “inside-out” heating is far more efficient as
it minimizes direct surface heat loss and delivers thermal energy directly to the water
stored in its immediate vicinity (Supplementary Fig. 35).

in heterogeneous structure and homogeneous structure.
This fundamental difference in heat management directly impacts the desorption
kinetics, as illustrated in Figure 5f (Fig. R4b). We define the “desorption onset” not as
a single temperature point, but as the initiation of a sustained, high-rate mass loss
phase. Re-examining Figure 5c, f (Fig. R4a, b), we observe that for the internal heating
(heterogeneous) structure, the curve immediately adopts a steep, linear slope, indicating
that efficient desorption begins almost instantaneously upon illumination. The system
wastes little energy on simply heating the bulk material; instead, the localized internal
heat immediately drives water evaporation. Conversely, the surface heating
(homogeneous) structure exhibits a distinct initial phase of very slow mass change, a
“thermal lag” period, before the slope steepens (Fig. R4c). This lag corresponds to the
time required for the inefficiently conducted surface heat to penetrate the gel and raise
the internal temperature sufficiently to initiate significant evaporation. Therefore, the
“desorption onset” is effectively immediate for our internal heating design, while it
is significantly delayed in the surface heating case, providing clear, kinetic evidence
for the superiority of the heterogeneous architecture. These clarifications, supported by
both kinetic data and direct thermal imaging, will be integrated into the manuscript to
strengthen our argument.

Reviewer #3
General Comment:
The manuscript (NCOMMS-25-72438-T) presents heterogeneous hygroscopic gels for
atmospheric water harvesting with seemingly impressive performance metrics, but
there are substantial concerns regarding the novelty of the approach, the robustness of
the main conclusions, and the practical scalability of the material. Moreover, significant
additional experiments are required to support the authors’ claims. Given the scope of
these issues, I recommend rejection in its current form.
Our responses to the comments and suggestions from Reviewer #3
We sincerely thank reviewer #3 for their valuable feedback and for recognizing the core
concept of our work. We have carefully considered the reviewer’s primary concerns
regarding the novelty, robustness, and scalability of our work. In response, we have
conducted a comprehensive suite of new experiments designed to provide unequivocal,
quantitative support for our central claims. The new data, which includes XRD,
low-field NMR, and extensive material stability and water quality analyses, now provides a
much deeper mechanistic insight and practical validation that we believe addresses all
points raised.
The central novelty of this work is the design of a heterogeneous structure that
spatially decouples the thermodynamic process of vapor sorption from the kinetic
process of liquid water transport. This is a fundamental departure from conventional
homogeneous structure, where these two functions are inherently coupled within a
single homogeneous matrix, leading to a performance trade-off. The core strategy
materializes the concept of asymmetric hydrophilicity-driven fast water diffusion by
establishing a localized hydrophilicity gradient. This is achieved by interfacing a super-
hygroscopic pectin-glycerol capture layer with a network of relatively hydrophobic
graphene oxide nanochannels, which serve as a low-resistance transport pathway,
thereby enabling rapid water diffusion.
This asymmetric hydrophilicity-driven fast water diffusion creates a directed,
high-flux pathway for water, which is mechanistically distinct from homogeneous
hydrophilic networks. We have now provided direct experimental proof for this
mechanism. XRD data reveals a dynamic expansion of the GO interlayer spacing upon
hydration, confirming the activation of these nanochannels as physical conduits for
water. Crucially, low-field NMR spectroscopy analysis quantitatively differentiates
between the intermediate water state within the hygroscopic capture layer and the free,
mobile water within the transport channels. The results clearly show a rapid saturation
of the bound state followed by a dominant and sustained increase in the free water signal,
directly validating the proposed water transfer process.
To address the robustness of our conclusions, we have performed critical stability
and performance tests. Raman spectroscopy data confirms the chemical integrity of
the GO framework remains unchanged after repeated hygroscopic cycles. A key
practical concern with such gels is component leakage. We have now performed a
rigorous analysis of the harvested water using ICP-MS, GC-MS, and TOC
measurements. These highly sensitive tests show negligible organic or ionic content,
confirming the high stability of the crosslinked pectin-glycerol matrix and the purity of
the collected water. Furthermore, to demonstrate real-world applicability and move
beyond controlled laboratory conditions, we have included outdoor atmospheric
water harvesting results from dynamic, real-world environments. These field tests
validate our laboratory findings and demonstrate effective performance under
fluctuating conditions. Regarding scalability, our layer-by-layer fabrication relies on
well-established and repeatable coating and solution immersion techniques. The
scalability is now supported by new data showing excellent batch-to-batch
reproducibility of the material’s structure and hygroscopic performance, which is the
foundational requirement for any scalable manufacturing process. We are confident that
this substantial body of new experimental evidence provides the necessary support for
our claims and transforms the manuscript into a complete and robust scientific
contribution.
According to your meaningful comments, the point-to-point responses according
to your kind suggestions have been addressed substantially in the revised version of our
manuscript and are marked by giving the text a blue color. We hope our revised version
can be accepted by Nature Communications.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. We agree that a
rigorous comparison with previously reported heterogeneous and multi-layered systems
is crucial to contextualize the novelty and superiority of our design. To address this,
we have substantially revised the manuscript to include a detailed comparative analysis.
This analysis not only contrasts our work with simple homogeneous blends but also
benchmarks it against the state-of-the-art structural designs in the field, including
Aligned Hierarchical, Unidirectional, Pore-engineered, Microsphere-based, and
Janus structures, many of which utilize materials like cellulose and sodium alginate.
As shown in Table 3 and Supplementary Fig. 24, our material consistently exhibits a
higher water sorption capacity than prominent benchmark materials. This superior
performance is a direct result of the fundamental advantages offered by our
“asymmetric hydrophilicity-driven decoupling” design.
Our approach is conceptually distinct from other advanced architectures. While
designs such as pore-engineered or aligned structures attempt to optimize transport by
creating predefined pathways, they do so within a single, swellable hygroscopic matrix
and thus remain fundamentally limited by the material’s intrinsic diffusion resistance.
In stark contrast, our superior performance is achieved through a macro-level
heterogeneous design concept without resorting to such complex microstructural
engineering. We have not performed any modifications like pore etching, chemical
grafting, or forced alignment within the GO transport layer. Instead, the remarkable
performance stems directly from our macro-level heterogeneous design concept—the
strategic lamination of two materials with a sharp, engineered hydrophilic gradient. The
fact that this relatively simple, scalable fabrication method yields results superior to
more intricate micro-engineered systems powerfully validates the effectiveness and
elegance of our core design principle.

This engineered disparity in hydrophilicity drives the core mechanism of our
HPGP. The outer pectin layer acts as a high-efficiency capture zone, rapidly condensing
atmospheric vapor into liquid. Subsequently, this difference in water affinity, further
amplified by glycerol, generates a powerful chemical potential gradient that actively
“pumps” the captured liquid from the pectin interface into the GO interlayers for rapid
diffusion and storage. This mechanism is directly supported by our molecular dynamics
(MD) simulations, which confirm high-velocity water diffusion along the GO
nanosheets—a diffusion coefficient significantly higher than that in comparable
homogeneous materials. This asymmetric hydrophilic design creates an unobstructed
pathway for water molecules, providing a solution to the contradiction between rapid
capture and slow transmission faced by traditional moisture-absorbing materials. By
spatially decoupling these two functions, it synergistically enhances adsorption
capacity and diffusion kinetics, thereby improving the water collection performance of
the material.
Furthermore, the selection of pectin was an evidence-based choice critical to
realizing this asymmetric concept. Our comparative study (Supplementary Fig. 8)
reveals that pectin possesses a superior combination of properties. Its exceptional
hygroscopicity enables gas-to-liquid conversion and the formation of visible water
droplets in just 11 minutes—a rate significantly faster than that of sodium alginate (50
minutes). This rapid capture ability is critical for establishing the strong concentration
gradient that drives subsequent transport. Moreover, unlike materials such as PVA and
KGM which failed to form stable films, pectin’s excellent film-forming capability
ensures the creation of a uniform, discrete surface layer. This processability is key to
achieving true physical separation between the capture and transport zones, thereby
preventing the polymer from intercalating into and obstructing the GO nanochannels.
Therefore, the combination of pectin’s superior kinetics and ideal processing
characteristics makes our novel asymmetric design possible, leading to a synergistic
enhancement of the material’s overall water-harvesting performance.

Response to comment 2:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. To experimentally validate the
asymmetric diffusion mechanism predicted by our molecular dynamics simulations, we
have conducted low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF-NMR) T relaxation
2
experiments. This technology non-destructively differentiates water populations based
on molecular mobility, classifying them according to their relaxation times: 0.1–10 ms
for bound water, 10–100 ms for intermediate water, and >100 ms for free water (Fig.
R5). We analyzed three key sample groups: the HPGP at different hydration levels
(initial, 30% RH, and 90% RH), and two control samples—pure glycerol-intercalated
pectin and pure glycerol-intercalated GO—both analyzed at initial and 90% RH
conditions.

molecules of hydrogel.
The results, as detailed below and shown in the T relaxation spectra
2
(Supplementary Fig. 13), provide direct and compelling experimental support for our
proposed mechanism.
1) HPGP (Heterogeneous Structure) Confirms the Multi-State Water Sorption
Process (Supplementary Fig. 13d)
At 30% RH, the T spectrum of HPGP is dominated by peaks at very short
2
relaxation times (<10 ms). This is the classic signature of bound water, confirming our
hypothesis that initial water uptake involves strong immobilization via hydrogen
bonding within the highly hydrophilic pectin layers.
At 90% RH, a dramatic change is observed. While the bound water peaks remain,
a new, distinct, and substantial peak emerges at a much longer T relaxation time (>100
2
ms). This peak is the unambiguous signature of free water. This directly demonstrates
that once the primary binding sites in the pectin are saturated, excess water transitions
into a high-mobility state, which, according to our model, resides within the GO
interlayer channels. This two-stage appearance of distinct water populations strongly
supports the proposed decoupling of water capture (binding) and transport (free).
2) Control Experiments Clarify the Roles of Pectin and GO (Supplementary Fig.
13a, b)
To further prove the spatial decoupling of these functions, we analyzed the
components separately:
Glycerol-Pectin: The Glycerol-Pectin matrix already displays a prominent T
2
peak in the intermediate range (10–100 ms). This signal is primarily attributed to the
liquid glycerol itself, which is intercalated within the pectin network, forming a baseline
fluidic system. Upon hydration to 90% RH, a critical phenomenon is observed. Instead
of creating a more mobile phase, the influx of water molecules forms strong hydrogen
bonds with both pectin and glycerol, creating a highly viscous ternary hydrogel. This is
evidenced by the fact that the T peak does not shift to longer times; instead, it remains
2
within the intermediate range, signifying that the overall molecular mobility is severely
restricted by the swollen polymer network. This result demonstrates the inherent
limitation of a purely hygroscopic polymer system: while it has high capacity, it traps
water in a high-viscosity, gel-like state, thus impeding rapid transport.
Glycerol-GO Interlayers: In stark contrast, the hydrated GO-only sample’s
signal is centered primarily in the intermediate range but with limited free water
character, indicating that atmospheric moisture merely wets the graphene surfaces
without filling the nanocapillaries to a bulk state. This proves that without the pump
effect of the pectin reservoir, the GO channels cannot achieve their full transport
potential.
3) Dynamic Water Exchange Validates Interconnectivity
An even more subtle but powerful piece of evidence comes from the evolution of
the bound water peaks. As the system hydrates from 30% to 90% RH, the peak
corresponding to weakly bound water (~10 ms) in HPGP actually decreases in
amplitude, while the free water peak grows enormously. This phenomenon is a hallmark
of dynamic exchange between water populations. It indicates that the bound water in
the pectin layers is not isolated but is in rapid exchange with the free water in the GO
channels. This confirms the seamless and efficient transfer of water from the capture
sites to the transport network, which forms the basis of our asymmetric diffusion
mechanism.
In summary, the LF-NMR results provide a multi-faceted experimental validation
of our proposed mechanism (Supplementary Fig. 13). They not only distinguish and
quantify the existence of both bound and free water but also, through the analysis of the
complete HPGP and its individual components, spatially assign the roles of water
capture to the pectin shell and rapid transport to the GO interlayers. The evidence of
dynamic exchange further confirms the efficient coupling between these two functions.
This body of experimental data is in excellent agreement with our simulation results
and supports the central claims of our manuscript.
By integrating our computational and experimental findings, we can draw a
cohesive and strongly supported conclusion. The LF-NMR results provide direct
experimental proof of the existence of two distinct water populations—bound and
free—within the HPGP material, with the free water population emerging at high
hydration levels. This aligns perfectly with the insights from our MD simulations. As
stated in our manuscript: “Our analysis (Fig. 3d, e and Supplementary Fig. 12) shows
that the diffusion coefficient D of water molecules in heterogeneous structure is
approximately 204.03, significantly higher than that in homogeneous structure (around
181.16).” The high-velocity diffusion pathway predicted by the simulations is the
microscopic origin of the highly mobile free water population detected by LF-NMR.
Thus, the synergy between direct experimental observation and atomistic simulation
provides compelling validation for our “asymmetric hydrophilicity-driven decoupling
design.” The LF-NMR data confirms what is happening (the existence of two water
states), while the MD simulations explain why it is happening (the creation of low-
friction GO nanochannels). This combined evidence provides strong support for our
hypothesis that the spatial decoupling of water capture (bound water in pectin) and
transport (free water in GO) effectively mitigates the inherent trade-off between
sorption capacity and diffusion kinetics in hygroscopic materials.

intermediate range, signifying that the overall molecular mobility is severely restricted
by the swollen polymer network. This result powerfully demonstrates the inherent
limitation of a purely hygroscopic polymer system: while it has high capacity, it traps
water in a high-viscosity, gel-like state, thus impeding rapid transport.
Conversely, Glycerol-GO interlayers also exhibit a signal centered primarily in the
intermediate range but with lower amplitude and limited free water character. This
indicates that without the driving force of an external reservoir, atmospheric moisture
merely wets the graphene surfaces and forms hydration layers, without filling the
nanocapillaries to a bulk state.
Building on these baselines, the HPGP structure reveals a transformative synergy.
At low humidity (30% RH), the spectrum resembles the pectin control, confirming
initial uptake is driven by the coating. However, at 90% RH, a dramatic evolution
occurs. A distinct, high-amplitude free water peak (>100 ms) emerges, which is
physically distinct from the constrained “swollen water” observed in the pure pectin
control. This implies a reservoir-to-channel mechanism: the pectin layer captures
moisture into its hydrogel network, but instead of stagnating in this restricted state, the
water is effectively pumped into the low-friction GO interlayers. This transition
converts semi-constrained moisture into a high-speed, bulk-like fluid, validating the
asymmetric diffusion mechanism proposed in our simulations.”
Comment 3:
The authors claim that glycerol does not evaporate during solar desorption based on
FTIR of evaporated gas. This is insufficient. Long-term cycling tests under realistic
outdoor conditions with quantitative analysis of glycerol loss (e.g., via HPLC or GC-
MS) are necessary to validate the material's durability.
Response to comment 3:
We appreciate the insightful feedback from the reviewer regarding the long-term
stability and potential loss of glycerol, which is a critical aspect of the practical
application of the material. The suggestion to employ a more quantitative and sensitive
technique is well-taken. In response to this valid point, we have conducted further
experiments to rigorously assess the stability of glycerol within our system during
the solar desorption process. To achieve this, we conducted an extended durability
test for 45 consecutive days of adsorption-desorption cycles. The samples maintained
morphological stability and consistent moisture absorption effects before and after the
hygroscopic cycles (Supplementary Fig. 53). Following this long-term cycling, we
collected the produced water from the solar desorption process and analyzed it using
Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS), a highly sensitive method for
detecting trace organic compounds. The GC-MS results show no characteristic peaks
corresponding to glycerol or its thermal decomposition products (Supplementary
Figs. 48-50). The primary components detected were residual atmospheric gases such
as oxygen and carbon monoxide. The absence of a glycerol signal in the GC-MS
analysis provides direct evidence that glycerol remains stable and does not evaporate
or decompose under the operational conditions of solar-driven desorption.
To properly incorporate this new evidence into the manuscript and address the
reviewer’s concern, we have revised the relevant section. The original text has been
updated to include the methodology and findings from the GC-MS analysis.

The water uptake of 0.83 g g⁻¹ at 30% RH is modest and not competitive with state-of-

Response to comment 4:
We thank the reviewer for their critical evaluation, which has prompted us to more
precisely define the optimal operating conditions and primary contributions of our work.
We agree that the water uptake at 30% RH is not record-setting when compared to
sorbents specifically engineered for extreme arid conditions (e.g., certain MOFs or salt-
based composites). Our work was not intended to compete on this single metric, and
we acknowledge that our initial presentation may have created this ambiguity. Instead,
our design philosophy prioritizes a unique and powerful combination of attributes
tailored for a different, yet arguably broader and more practical, application
scenario.
The strategic advantage of our HPGP sorbent lies not in extreme-RH performance,
but in its exceptional balance of high capacity, rapid kinetics, low-energy
regeneration, and robust stability under the mid-to-high humidity conditions (RH >
40%) that characterize the vast majority of the world’s populated regions. While some
state-of-the-art sorbents exhibit higher equilibrium capacities at low RH, they often face
critical trade-offs that limit their practical deployment. For instance, hygroscopic salts
suffer from deliquescence and leakage, compromising cyclability, while many MOFs
require energy-intensive synthesis and regeneration. [1,2] The HPGP is specifically
engineered to circumvent these issues, offering a scalable and durable solution for
the climates where most people live.
Furthermore, we wish to emphasize that a core scientific contribution of our work
is the development of an asymmetric hydrophilic structural design that
dramatically enhances sorption/desorption kinetics. By strategically creating a
highly hydrophilic outer layer and a relatively less hydrophilic inner core, we engineer
a distinct vapor pressure gradient that actively pulls water molecules from the surface
deep into the material’s matrix. This design provides a new solution to the critical
transport challenge faced by traditional hydrogel adsorbents with homogeneous
structures. This strategy of using engineered hydrophilicity gradients to boost dynamic
performance holds broad relevance and can be applied to other liquid sorbent-based gel
systems. Therefore, our work’s primary value should be seen not just in achieving a
specific uptake value, but in providing a robust and scalable method to engineer a
superior balance of capacity, kinetics, and stability, tailored for efficient water
harvesting in the climates where most people live.
To provide a clearer perspective on the performance of the HPGP, we have now
included a comparative table in the revised manuscript (Table.2). This table
benchmarks our HPGP sorbent against a range of representative state-of-the-art
materials (including select MOFs, hygroscopic salt composites, and advanced
hydrogels). This comparison will explicitly highlight that while our material may not
lead in equilibrium capacity alone, its overall combination of good uptake, fast kinetics
and low-energy regeneration makes it a highly competitive and promising candidate for
practical solar-driven atmospheric water harvesting applications.

Comment 5:
The photothermal conversion efficiency of GO is well-known. The manuscript fails to
demonstrate how the HPGP structure enhances this property beyond what is expected
from GO alone. Spectral reflectance and thermal imaging under controlled conditions
could be provided to substantiate claims of improved light trapping.
Response to comment 5:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. To experimentally isolate the
contribution of the material’s morphology, we designed a specific control experiment.
By comparing the wrinkled HPGP against a flat counterpart (a ‘Pectin-flat GO
interlayers-Pectin’ film), we demonstrate that the wrinkled surface is the primary driver
for the observed enhancement in light absorption and photothermal performance.
The underlying physical mechanism for this improvement was quantified using
UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 26, while the Pectin-flat
GO interlayers-Pectin already demonstrated a high broadband solar absorbance of
90.1%, the wrinkled HPGP structure achieved an exceptional 96.9%. This significant
~7% increase is a direct consequence of the wrinkles functioning as an efficient light-
trapping structure. On a conventional flat surface, a notable fraction of incident light is
immediately lost to specular reflection. In contrast, the wrinkled HPGP’s randomly
oriented surface normals redirect incident photons. Instead of reflecting back into the
environment, light striking a sloped surface is preferentially scattered deeper into
adjacent wrinkle valleys. This initial suppression of reflective loss is critical. Once
trapped within this topography, the photons undergo multiple internal reflections,
dramatically extending their optical path length within the absorbing GO medium. At
each reflection, a portion of the light energy is absorbed, increasing the cumulative
probability of absorption toward unity. In essence, the wrinkled geometry transforms
the material into a more effective optical cavity, minimizing energy loss and
maximizing solar energy harvesting. [1,2]
Supplementary Fig. 26 UV-Vis-NIR absorption characteristics of HPGP and Pectin-flat GO
interlayers-Pectin.
To directly visualize and quantify the impact of this enhanced absorption on
thermal performance, we conducted thermal imaging under simulated solar irradiation.
The results demonstrate that under the same intensity conditions (1 sun, AM 1.5G),
the HPGP sample reached a higher steady-state temperature more quickly than the Pectin-
flat GO interlayers-Pectin (Supplementary Fig. 33). As solar intensity increased (from
0.7 sun to 1.6 sun), the HPGP sample also exhibited a higher steady-state temperature
(Supplementary Figs. 28, 30 and 31). This enhanced heat generation directly correlates
with the increased solar absorbance previously discussed. The results confirm that the
wrinkled morphology is not merely a passive surface feature but an active light-trapping
structure that significantly amplifies the photothermal conversion efficiency of the
material.

Comment 6:
The fabrication process involves multiple steps (layer-by-layer assembly, crosslinking,
solvent exchange) that are difficult to scale. The authors should discuss the
reproducibility of the wrinkle structure, layer uniformity, and the feasibility of mass
production.
Response to comment 6:
Thank you for this constructive comment. Based on the current manuscript and
supplementary information, we agree that the feasibility of the multi-step preparation
process in terms of reproducibility and scalability needs to be more clearly elucidated.
In the revision, we will thoroughly explain the steps to ensure control over the wrinkled
structure and layer uniformity and the steps to transform the experimental procedure
into a continuous production process.
First, concerning the reproducibility of the crucial wrinkle structure, we can
confirm its high consistency over extended periods. The formation of these wrinkles is
governed by a well-understood physical mechanism: strain mismatch arising from the
iterative drying and differential shrinkage of the GO layers. The primary determinants
of the wrinkle wavelength and amplitude are the material’s modulus and the final dry
film thickness, which are directly controlled by the GO solution concentration and the
number of deposition-drying cycles. Systematic experiments show that a four-layer
structure consistently forms the optimal wrinkle pattern. This conclusion is supported
by the macroscopic images of samples prepared at different times from December 2022
to the present, all of which exhibit a consistent wrinkle pattern (Supplementary Fig. 58).
Similarly, regarding layer uniformity, we have conducted rigorous quality control
throughout our research. Thickness measurements of the GO base films, also performed
on samples from different batches over the same extended timeframe, confirm excellent
uniformity with minimal deviation (Supplementary Fig. 59). This consistency
underscores the robustness of our layer-by-layer assembly protocol, where controlled
solution spreading and drying steps ensure a uniform deposition process.
Supplementary Fig. 58 From December 2022 to December 2025, the GO film has a stable wrinkle
structure.
Supplementary Fig. 59 The GO film from December 2022 to December 2025 has a uniform
thickness.
Finally, we have carefully considered the feasibility of mass production and
envision a clear pathway to translate our laboratory-scale “spread-dry-repeat” method
into an industrially relevant, continuous process. The four-layer GO base film can be
formed using established techniques such as spray/blade coating or slot-die coating,
coupled with a multi-zone hot-air drying system to perform the iterative deposition
cycles. Following the formation of the base film, the surface pectin layers would be
applied to both sides using a similar coating process. Subsequently, the
functionalization steps can be adapted to an in-line configuration: the cross-linking
would occur in a short-residence-time anhydrous zinc acetate bath, and the final
glycerol solvent exchange could be managed in a counter-current washing cascade to
enhance throughput and reduce solvent consumption.
It is important to highlight that all the aforementioned steps—coating, multi-zone
drying, and immersion baths—are standard unit operations within the membrane and
coating industries. Key process parameters such as coating speed, drying temperature
and humidity, and residence time can be precisely controlled to replicate the thermal
history and layering effect achieved in our lab (e.g., each layer of GO film is dried in
an oven at 75 °C for 75 minutes. After coating with a pectin layer, it is crosslinked in a
zinc acetate solution for 10 minutes. Solvent replacement is carried out in glycerol for
24 hours). To ensure quality assurance in a scaled-up process, in-line metrology tools—
such as mass-per-area sensors, and optical texture analysis for wrinkle statistics—can
provide closed-loop feedback for process control.
Given that our entire process utilizes aqueous solutions, operates at ambient or
mild temperatures, and requires no high-vacuum or cleanroom facilities, we are
confident that scaling this fabrication from centimeter-sized lab samples to meter-scale
roll-to-roll production is engineeringly feasible. While we refrain from adding new
scale-up data in the current manuscript to maintain focus, we have supplemented the
methods section with more explicit process parameters and quality control metrics. This
will ensure that our peers can readily replicate the material’s unique morphology and
high performance under equivalent conditions.

Comment 7:
The outdoor test was conducted only under moderate RH (72–82.6%) and temperature
(23–31°C). Performance under extreme conditions (e.g., arid or highly humid climates)
is not demonstrated, limiting the generalizability of the conclusions.
Response to Comment 7:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the operational scope
of the HPGP system. The initial outdoor test was indeed conducted under a specific set
of moderate conditions, and we agree that demonstrating its performance across a wider
climatic range is essential to validate its generalizability. To achieve this, we conducted
two multi-day outdoor experiments. However, due to current environmental constraints,
we performed the experiments in cooler, high-humidity conditions as well as in warmer,
drier conditions.
The first experiment was conducted in a cooler, high-humidity climate. Over three
days, the ambient temperature reached a maximum of 16 °C and a minimum of 7.6 °C.
The average temperature fluctuated between 8.8 °C and 13.1 °C. The relative humidity
varied significantly, with a minimum of 62.6% and a peak of 92%, while the average
humidity ranged from 68.1% to 84.7% (Supplementary Fig. 42). Despite the lower

We sincerely agree with the insightful comments regarding water quality and recognize
that quantitative analysis is crucial for a comprehensive assessment of system safety
and practical viability.
To address this, we conducted supplementary tests and analyses on the collected
water. The analysis includes ICP-MS to measure the concentration of key metal ions,
and Total Organic Carbon (TOC) analysis, which can represent the total amount of
organic matter. The ICP-MS test indicated that the concentrations of various key metal
ions, particularly zinc (Zn2+) used for cross-linking, were far below the safe drinking

in the collected water was found to be exceptionally low (<5 mg/L), which is
comparable to that of deionized water and further confirms the absence of leached
organic matter (Fig. 6e).
The glycerol is securely immobilized within the HPGP material through both
hydrogen bonding and chemical crosslinking. This robust immobilization prevents it
from being carried over with water vapor during desorption, even across multiple
sorption-desorption cycles. Similarly, the chemically crosslinked zinc ions remain
stably fixed at the network nodes and do not leach into the collected water. To enhance
the rigor and completeness of the manuscript, we will explicitly analyze the data
obtained from GC-MS, ICP-MS, and TOC data in the main text, thereby providing
authoritative quantitative support for the environmental safety of the materials and the
purity of the produced water.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The revised manuscript and supporting information incorporate several important improvements, particularly in structural characterization (XRD, Raman, TEM), analytical techniques (ICP-MS, TOC, GC-MS), and methodological detail in the MD simulations. These changes strengthen the experimental foundation of the work.

However, a number of key issues identified in the previous review remain insufficiently addressed. In particular, (1) validation of the proposed asymmetric-diffusion mechanism, (2) benchmarking against published sorbent systems under standardized conditions, (3) quantification of water purity, and (4) long-term environmental stability are still incomplete. These points are essential for fully supporting the manuscript’s conclusions and for aligning with the methodological standards expected in Nature Communications.

A further revision is therefore required before the manuscript can be considered suitable for publication.

Major Comments
1. Mechanism validation remains incomplete
Although the revised version includes XRD and Raman data, the mechanistic claim that asymmetric hydrophilicity drives preferential diffusion is still not fully supported experimentally.
Specifically:
XRD is presented under a single hydration state;
no SAXS or XRD measurements at low vs high RH (e.g., 30% vs 90% RH) are provided;
MD simulations remain unvalidated by any experimental technique capable of distinguishing bound vs free water.
Required revision:
Please include humidity-dependent structural data (XRD/SAXS) or, alternatively, provide an experimental proxy such as DSC, NMR, or dielectric spectroscopy to validate the MD-predicted hydration gradient.

2. Benchmarking against state-of-the-art remains insufficient
The performance comparison to literature values remains qualitative. While the Supporting Information includes additional
data, the comparison is still not standardized for RH, temperature, irradiance, and sample mass.
Required revision:
Provide a standardized benchmarking table under equivalent conditions (RH, temperature, cycle time, mass loading). This
should be placed in the main text. Please also moderate any claims of “high yield” or “fast diffusion” unless they are directly
demonstrated under comparable metrics.

3. Statistical reproducibility is inconsistently reported
The Supporting Information clarifies that n = 5 sets were used for several measurements, but the main text figures still lack:
error bars,
standard deviations or confidence intervals,
explicit n values, and
statistical treatment of variability.
Required revision:
All quantitative plots should include error bars and clearly specify sample size (n) in each figure caption. This is essential for
assessing reproducibility.

4. Long-term durability and environmental stability insufficiently addressed
The current stability data are limited to ~45 days and fungus tests. Critical environmental stressors—UV exposure, dust,
temperature cycling, humidity cycling—are not addressed.
Required revision:
Either expand the durability tests (UV, cycles, outdoor exposure) or provide a detailed discussion acknowledging these
limitations and their expected impact on real-world operation.

5. Water purity analysis requires full quantification
The addition of ICP-MS, TOC and GC-MS is a strong improvement, but the data remain largely qualitative.
Required revision:
Please report:
absolute concentrations (ppm or ppb) for each detected ion/compound,
limits of detection (LOD) for each analytical method,
explicit quantification of Zn or other potential leachates.
This is necessary to support any claims regarding water safety or purity.

6. Cost and scalability discussion is missing
Given the practical orientation of atmospheric water harvesting, a minimal discussion of materials cost, scalability and
recyclability is essential.
Required revision:
Please add a brief subsection addressing feasibility, scaling challenges, and material sustainability.

Minor Comments
Improve resolution and font sizes in schematic and microscopic figures; several panels remain hard to read.
Ensure consistency in terminology (GO interlayers, pectin-GO gradient, GOGEL structures).
Provide more descriptive captions in the Supporting Information, especially where multiple curves or conditions are shown.
Moderate speculative statements about large-scale implementation unless supported by data.

Summary
The manuscript has improved substantially, particularly in analytical rigor and methodological clarity. However, several
critical points—mechanistic validation, benchmarking, statistical reproducibility, water purity quantification, and
environmental stability—remain unresolved. Addressing these issues will significantly strengthen the manuscript and align it
with Nature Communications standards.
I would be pleased to review a thoroughly revised version.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Hygroscopic polymeric gels hold a promising avenue for sustainable sorption-based atmospheric water harvesting (SAWH). However, conventional designs relying on homogeneous hydrophilic networks face an inherent trade-off: strong hydrogen bond-mediated water retention and osmotic pressure-driven water transport. Here, we propose a strategy to construct heterogeneous structure composed of hydrophilic pectin shell and relatively hydrophobic graphene oxide (GO) sheets core for hygroscopic polymeric organgel integrated with glycerol. The pectin shell acts as a gas–liquid conversion interface, enabling continuous and efficient water condensation. The incorporation of pristine GO interlayers significantly reduces the interaction between adsorbed water molecules and hydrophilic functional groups. This configuration enhances glycerol-enabled osmotic pumping for rapid water transport into storage and supports efficient solar-driven water release. The resulting organgel exhibits a high water uptake capacity ranging from 0.83 to 6.57 g g-1 across a broad relative humidity spectrum (30% to 90%). Under 1.0 sun illumination, it achieves a notable desorption rate of 2.06 kg m-2 h-1, contributing to a daily water yield of up to 2.86 L kg -1day-1. This heterogeneous structure challenges the conventional paradigm of water sorbent maximizing hydrophilicity and supports the rational design of high-performance toward next-generation SAWH materials.

---

## Introduction

Atmospheric water vapor as a vast yet underutilized freshwater source, holds three times the volume of all polar ice caps and rivers1,2. To effectively harness this moisture resource, sorption-based atmospheric water harvesting technology offers a sustainable solution applicable across diverse climates and geographical locations3,4. Typical sorbent materials, such as pore-confining hollow matrices5, linker-extended MOFs6, and capillary force-mediated fiber scaffolds7, have shown fast sorption kinetics but reached low moisture retention capacity owing to their non-swelling property. For sustainable hygroscopic capability, polymeric gels are emerging as promising candidate due to their chemically designable hydrophilic structure, reversible swollen capability, and high accessibility8,9. The alternative introduction of hygroscopic solid salts (e.g., LiCl, CaCl2, etc.)10,11 or liquid solvents (e.g., glycerol, ionic liquid, etc)8,12 into the polymeric crosslinked network can further enhance the sorption capacity. In a typical hygroscopic process, moisture is initially converted to the liquid state via a multistage sorption mechanism involving both chemisorption and deliquescence13. Subsequently, the liquid water molecules are gradually transported into the interior polymeric network driven by osmotic pressure, thereby reactivating the hygroscopic sites exposed to the surface of gels (Fig. 1a).

Conventional polymeric hygroscopic system focuses on constructing homogeneous porous structures, which suffer from low mass transfer velocity due to the strong interaction between hydrophilic polymer chains and water molecules14,15. Notably, a fundamental trade-off exists between chemical sorption and osmotic pressure transportation, in which hydrophilic chains can accelerate the moisture sorption, but reduce the water transportation velocity. To solve this issue, a series of pore engineering strategies (e.g., cryogelation5, foaming-drying16, templating17, vertical freezing18, bidirectional freezing19, etc.) are developed to enhance mass transfer kinetics by constructing a variety of macroscale, interconnected, vertically aligned and bidirectionally aligned pores for high capillary force. However, the optimal criteria for pore size and distribution are unclear and hard to achieve the structural balance between sorption and desorption processes. In addition, controllable and reliable fabrication strategies in a cost-effective and scalable way are highly urgent to achieve.

Here we propose a strategy to construct heterogeneous structure composed of pectin-graphene oxide (GO)-pectin-based hygroscopic organogel (HPGP) uniformly infused with glycerol, with high sorption capacity and rapid desorption rates. This structure achieves spatial decoupling of water capture and transport. The outer pectin-glycerol layers provide the thermodynamic driving force for vapor liquefaction via a strong osmotic gradient, while the central GO interlayers establish a kinetic pathway to sustain the process. Acting as a low-friction internal transport network, GO interlayers prevent surface saturation by rapidly channeling condensed water into the material’s core. This spatial decoupling prevents the captured water molecules from being overly immobilized by hydrogen bonds at the surface, thereby sustaining the high efficiency of the glycerol-driven osmotic pump. Additionally, the central GO interlayers exhibit a strong photothermal response and enable solar-driven water release, significantly boosting the overall desorption efficiency. As a result, HPGP achieves a high sorption capacity, ranging from 0.83 to 6.57 g g-1 at relative humidities of 30% to 90%; under 1.0 sun illumination, the desorption rate was up to 2.06 kg m-2 h-1, and more than 90% of the water was desorbed within 40 min. These features enable a HPGP-based SAWH device to produce up to 2.86 L water kg sorbent -1day-1, representing a performance highly competitive with the leading reported SAWH systems. This work provides valuable insights into designing high-performance sorbent materials and highlights a promising strategy to enhance moisture sorption-desorption performance in SAWH applications.
